abstract: Abstract Resistance to anti-angiogenic therapy remains a major obstacle in non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Although bevacizumab effectively neutralizes VEGFA and suppresses neovascularization, its clinical benefit is often transient. Here, we demonstrate that VEGFA inhibition paradoxically intensifies intratumoral hypoxia, leading to stabilization of HIF1A and activation of a compensatory pro-malignant program. Increased HIF1A not only enhances tumor cell migration, epithelial–mesenchymal transition, and chemoresistance, but also upregulates CD105 (Endoglin), a hypoxia-responsive pro-angiogenic mediator that attenuates the anti-vascular effects of bevacizumab. Thus, anti-VEGFA therapy initiates a hypoxia-driven HIF1A–CD105 axis that sustains tumor aggressiveness and vascular adaptation despite VEGFA blockade. We identify the pre–miR-16-1 duplex as a physiological dual-regulatory system capable of simultaneously targeting this adaptive circuit. The guide strand miR-16-5p directly represses VEGFA, recapitulating the anti-angiogenic action of bevacizumab. In contrast, the passenger strand miR-16-1-3p suppresses HIF1A expression, thereby preventing hypoxia-induced malignant phenotypes and limiting CD105 upregulation. Functional analyses revealed that VEGFA inhibition was accompanied by HIF1A upregulation, while elevated HIF1A promoted cell migration, mesenchymal-like changes, and cisplatin resistance. Co-expression of miR-16-1-3p suppressed HIF1A and attenuated these adverse phenotypes. In a chick chorioallantoic membrane xenograft model, dual regulation of VEGFA and HIF1A markedly reduced vascular density, tumor growth, and metastatic dissemination compared with single anti-angiogenic intervention. Collectively, our findings uncover a hypoxia-mediated resistance mechanism driven by the HIF1A–CD105 axis following VEGFA inhibition and establish the cooperative function of the miR-16 duplex as a strategy to concurrently suppress angiogenesis and its adaptive hypoxic feedback. Concurrent targeting of VEGFA and HIF1A may therefore provide a strategy to enhance the antitumor efficacy of anti-angiogenic therapy in NSCLC.

title: Targeting common denominators of DNA damage tolerance mechanisms as therapeutic strategy to cope with dynamic phenotypic changes in triple-negative breast cancer cells
abstract: Abstract Triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the most aggressive type of breast cancer with limited treatment options and a propensity towards chemoresistance. Given the lack of targetable receptors, treatment relies primarily on chemotherapy. While mechanisms leading to chemoresistance are vastly unknown, DNA damage tolerance (DDT) pathways have emerged as potential drivers of chemoresistance. Herein, we report a phenotypic characterization of four TNBC- and six non-TNBC cell lines, which supports the relevance of DDT in the TNBC response to chemotherapy. We unveiled an association between DDT pathway activation through PCNA-ubiquitination, augmented epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and stemness features, specifically in 3D spheroid culture from TNBC cells. Analysis of replication dynamics revealed a pronounced replication slowdown in 3D- versus 2D-cultured TNBC but not in non-TNBC cells. The exploration of DDT pathway usage in three TNBC cell lines (MDA-MB-231, Hs578t, MDA-MB-468) uncovers reliance on ZRANB3-, HLTF- and SMARCAL1-dependent fork reversal in 3D, while translesion DNA synthesis (TLS) polymerases (POLs) were more active under 2D conditions. Screening cytotoxicity with a panel of ten drugs targeting key DDT pathway components identified POLζ inhibition (JH-RE-06; IC 50 ≤ 7 µM/48 h) and CHK1 inhibition (PF477736; IC 50 ≤ 20 µM/48 h) as the most potent single-agent treatments in all three cell lines under both conditions. Mechanistically, both POLζ and CHK1 inhibition target several DDT pathways, in sum, causing replication slowdown, revealed consistently for CHK1. While TNBC cell lines were largely unresponsive to Olaparib mono-treatment, especially in 3D culture, all three cell lines were resensitized by combining Olaparib with low-dose POLζ-, CHK1-, or RAD51 inhibitor, except for 3D-cultured MDA-MB-231 cells, which may resist Olaparib due to their high ZRANB3 complex formation in the nucleus. These findings identify key DDT pathway components such as POLζ and CHK1 as druggable targets that alone or in combination with Olaparib may overcome chemoresistance in TNBC.

title: New Δ246p53 isoform responds to DNA damage to enhance p53 family functions in cellular senescence
abstract: Abstract p53 is, without a doubt, one of the most powerful genes in our genome, as it makes growth vs arrest, repair vs replacement, catabolism vs anabolism, life vs death decisions in the cell. An alteration or malfunction in p53 may lead to cancer, degeneration or premature ageing. So, it is not surprising that p53 is also one of the most complex and tightly regulated genes, encoding for at least 10 RNA variants and 12 widely accepted protein forms. Here we identify one new p53 protein isoform of approximately 18 kDa that we termed Δ246p53. Δ246p53 is translated from an alternative translation initiation site (TIS) at codon 246. TIS-246 is preceded by a strong Kozak sequence and appears conserved in vertebrates, from sea lamprey to humans. Δ246p53’s origin and expression in cells were confirmed by frameshift and start codon mutations; five different antibodies against epitopes spanning its N- to C-terminus, as well as an antibody against the DNA-binding domain region just upstream of its initiator methionine, which served as a negative control; and siRNAs and an antisense oligo targeting TIS-246, which knocked down Δ246p53 with little or no effect on full-length (FL) p53 protein levels. Δ246p53 was induced by DNA damage and triggered senescence and impaired tumour formation/growth in colony formation assays. Mechanistically, Δ246p53 interacted with FLp53, leading to a decrease in the expression of downstream target genes HDM2 and p21 . Concurrently, it also interacted with ΔNp63, leading to p53 -independent p63 -mediated activation of p21 , a known senescence activator. Our results unveil a new naturally occurring and tightly controlled factor with specific functions in p21 regulation and senescence. Future studies on Δ246p53 are likely to help us better understand and control the processes of tumour suppression and ageing.

title: p53 wild-type/low c-Myc-expressing ONS76 pediatric medulloblastoma cells become senescent after gamma-irradiation and can be eliminated by senolytic substances
abstract: Abstract Craniospinal irradiation (CSI) is an indispensable part of oncological treatment for pediatric medulloblastoma. However, despite significantly improving oncological outcome, it is also associated with severe short- and long-term side effects such as inflammation and impaired neurocognition. The presence of senescent cells has been identified as a potential contributing factor to these issues. In our study, we demonstrate that p53 wild-type and c-Myc-low-expressing ONS76 medulloblastoma cells underwent senescence, a terminal and stable cell cycle arrest, after exposure to gamma irradiation (γIR). In contrast, p53-mutated UW228-3 cells exhibited apoptosis following the same treatment. ONS76 cells displayed typical senescence properties, including cell and nuclei enlargement, an active DNA damage response with stabilization of p53 and increased expression of its target gene, the CDK inhibitor p21 WAF1/CIP1 , as well as elevated senescence-associated beta-galactosidase activity and lipofuscin accumulation. Knockdown of p53 or p21 expression with siRNAs abolished γIR-mediated senescence. Furthermore, overexpression of c-Myc resulted in a partial shift from senescence to cell death induction after γIR treatment, which was inhibited by using the caspase-inhibitor q-VD-OPh. The γIR-exposed ONS76 cells showed susceptibility to senolytic substances, such as the BCL-2 family inhibitor Navitoclax and the PI3K-inhibitors PX-866 and BAY80-6946, which specifically target senescent cells. In conclusion, employing senolytics on irradiated medulloblastoma cells with wild-type p53 and low c-Myc expression may lead to reduced therapeutic side effects as well as attenuate tumor relapse and potentially minimize CSI doses required for effective tumor cell elimination.

title: Small mitochondria-targeting compound SMIP004 selectively eliminates therapy-induced senescent tumor cells by blocking AMPK-dependent PDHA stabilization and improves the outcomes of chemotherapy
abstract: Abstract Therapy-induced senescence (TIS) contributes to tumor recurrence and metastasis. Selective elimination of TIS cells by senolytics would be beneficial for cancer treatment. Here, we found that the stabilization of PDHA (catalytic subunit of pyruvate dehydrogenase) in TIS cancer cells relies on the elevated activity of AMPK. A small-scale chemical screening in TIS cells identified SMIP004, a mitochondria-targeting compound, that can attenuate the PDHA stabilization by promoting the ubiquitin-mediated degradation of PDHA without affecting the activity of AMPK. Activation of AMPK by metformin also leads to the stabilization of ectopically expressed PDHA in proliferating cells, which can be attenuated by SMIP004 treatment or abolished by the substitution of AMPK phosphorylation sites on PDHA. Moreover, a low dose of SMIP004 exerts a selective killing of TIS cancer cells by inducing an energy crisis and massive apoptosis. Most importantly, SMIP004 combined with doxorubicin can suppress tumor growth, eliminate p21-positive cells, and reduce metastatic lesions in tumor-bearing mice. scRNA-seq analysis revealed that elevated transcription of PDHA is associated with senescence-like tumor cells. The expression of both PDHA and p21 is enhanced by chemotherapy and correlates with poor patient survival, implicating the therapeutic potential of targeting PDHA. As such, our findings demonstrated SMIP004 is a promising senolytic agent capable of selectively eliminating TIS cells by blocking the AMPK-mediated stabilization of PDHA.

title: An FXR-dependent cellular program for Kupffer cell pool restoration fuels liver regeneration
abstract: Abstract Liver transplantation and partial hepatectomy represent the most effective therapeutic strategies for end-stage liver diseases. However, persistent donor organ shortages have intensified clinical interest in interventions that enhance liver regeneration. The farnesoid X receptor (FXR) and Kupffer cells both play crucial roles in liver regeneration. This study, therefore, aims to investigate whether FXR regulates liver regeneration by maintaining the homeostasis of Kupffer cells. In a 70% partial hepatectomy model, we observed robust activation and increased infiltration of T cells and Kupffer cells in the regenerating livers of wild-type (WT) mice. In contrast, although FXR-deficient (FXR −/− ) mice exhibited elevated baseline levels of both T cells and Kupffer cells in the liver, their regenerating livers showed markedly attenuated immune cell activation and reduced infiltration. During liver regeneration, the restoration of the Kupffer cell pool is achieved through the recruitment of circulating monocytes and the proliferation of resident Kupffer cells. Our data demonstrate that FXR deficiency impairs both the migration of circulating monocytes into the regenerating liver and the proliferation of resident Kupffer cells. Consequently, delayed liver regeneration in FXR −/− mice is likely due to impaired recovery of the Kupffer cell pool and altered M1/M2 polarization. Mechanistically, FXR promotes monocyte migration by targeting Ccr2 and enhances Kupffer cell proliferation via the CSF1/PI3K/Akt signaling pathway, thereby synergistically facilitating the restoration of Kupffer cell pool homeostasis during liver regeneration. Additionally, impaired monocyte recruitment in aged mice may contribute to reduced regenerative capacity with aging. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that homeostatic restoration and functional activation of Kupffer cells are critically governed by FXR. This mechanistic insight highlights FXR-Kupffer cells as a central therapeutic target for enhancing liver repair.

title: A pan-cancer analysis of TLK1 and TLK2: genomic instability, immunomodulation, and therapeutic implications
abstract: Abstract Tousled-like kinases TLK1 and TLK2 are evolutionarily conserved serine/threonine kinases involved in the DNA damage response and cell cycle regulation; however, their pan-cancer molecular profiles and clinical relevance remain largely unexplored. By integrating multi-omics data from TCGA and GTEx across 33 cancer types, we demonstrate that TLK1 and TLK2 exhibit distinct expression patterns and are associated with patient prognosis in a cancer type-specific manner. Genetic alterations in TLK1 and TLK2 were frequently observed and significantly correlated with multiple markers of genomic instability, including tumor mutation burden, microsatellite instability, and homologous recombination deficiency. Functional experiments showed that knockdown of TLK1 or TLK2 in cancer cell lines markedly increased DNA damage, impaired cellular proliferation, and induced apoptosis, with TLK2 exhibiting a more prominent role in DNA repair processes. Furthermore, both kinases were negatively correlated with immune and stromal scores, and their expression levels were linked to specific immune cell subsets—positively with resting CD4 + T cells and macrophages, but negatively with CD8 + T cells and activated NK cells. Additional functional immune analyses revealed that TLK1/TLK2 expression correlated positively with immune exclusion signatures and MDSC infiltration, rather than with classical T-cell exhaustion markers. Multiplex immunohistochemistry in colorectal cancer tissues further resolved these associations into divergent phenotypes: TLK1-high tumors exhibited reduced T cell infiltration consistent with immune exclusion, whereas TLK2-high tumors showed Treg enrichment and CD39 upregulation indicative of an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Notably, TLK1 and TLK2 expression demonstrated predictive utility for responses to chemotherapy and immunotherapy across several malignancies. Our findings underscore the multifaceted roles of TLK1 and TLK2 in tumorigenesis and tumor immune modulation, supporting their potential as prognostic biomarkers and promising therapeutic targets in precision oncology.

title: Mitochondrial-derived peptide MOTS-c rescues vascular endothelial damage via PLA2G6 in diabetic retinopathy
abstract: Abstract As the predominant microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus that leads to blindness, diabetic retinopathy (DR) still presents a challenge due to the scarcity of effective therapeutic approaches, particularly in its early stage. Here, we observed that the expression of the mitochondrial open-reading-frame of the 12 S rRNA-c (MOTS-c), a mitochondrial-derived peptide, was predominantly localized in retinal endothelial cells. Thus, we combined genetic and pharmacological approaches in vivo and in vitro to explore whether vascular endothelial damage in DR is involved in MOTS-c dysregulation and its underlying mechanism. High glucose exposure reduced the expression of MOTS-c in retinal vasculature. While MOTS-c treatment protected endothelial barrier and ameliorated mitochondrial dysfunction in human retinal endothelial cells with high-glucose-induced injury and streptozotocin-induced diabetic mouse model. Furthermore, in vitro experiments were used to explore the underlying molecular mechanisms for rescuing vascular endothelial damage of MOTS-c. Transcriptomic analyses and lipidomic analyses showed that MOTS-c increased the phospholipase A2 activity and regulated phospholipid metabolism. Among the differentially expressed genes associated with upregulated phospholipase A2 activity, phospholipase A2 group VI (PLA2G6) exhibited the most significant upregulation following MOTS-c treatment. PLA2G6-mediated lipid peroxide degradation served as a primary mediator of protecting the retinal endothelial barrier during MOTS-c treatment, while knockdown of PLA2G6 blocked the protective effect of MOTS-c against vascular endothelial damage in vitro and in vivo. Taken together, our findings identified a novel role of MOTS-c dysregulation mediating vascular endothelial damage in DR and that MOTS-c supplementation was a potential therapeutic approach to regulating phospholipid homeostasis and protecting the endothelial barrier via PLA2G6 against DR.

title: Hepatic senescence triggered by statins decreases systemic IGF-1 signaling to drive skeletal muscle atrophy
abstract: Abstract Statins lower circulating cholesterol by inhibiting hepatic 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase (HMGCR). However, their clinical use is frequently limited by statin-associated muscle complications, the underlying mechanisms of which remain incompletely understood. Here we demonstrate that lovastatin and atorvastatin induce cellular senescence in hepatocytes and hepatic tissue, as evidenced by increased senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity and induction of the canonical markers p21 and p16. Among senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) was selectively and significantly reduced. In a transwell coculture system, senescent AML12 hepatocytes impaired C2C12 myogenesis, decreased myotube diameter, and upregulated the muscle atrophy markers Atrogin-1 and MuRF1. Consistent with these in vitro findings, in vivo lovastatin and ezetimibe (LE) exposure increased hepatic SA-β-gal-positive area, elevated p21/p16 expression, and lowered circulating IGF-1. Tibialis anterior muscle displayed reduced fiber cross-sectional area with a smaller-shifted size distribution, heightened atrophy signaling, and diminished AKT/mTOR pathway activation. Together, these findings support a liver-to-muscle endocrine axis in which lovastatin-induced hepatic senescence suppresses IGF-1, secondarily impairing myogenesis and promoting skeletal muscle atrophy via attenuation of AKT/mTOR signaling. Targeting hepatic senescence or restoring IGF-1/AKT/mTOR activity may offer therapeutic strategies to mitigate statin-associated myopathy.

title: Stress-induced eIF2α phosphorylation promotes tumor metastasis in oral squamous cell carcinoma
abstract: Abstract Stress granules (SGs) are non-membranous protein–RNA aggregates that form in the cytoplasm of mammalian cells under various stress conditions. In normal cells, SGs mitigate stress-induced damage by arresting translation. SGs have also been implicated in cancer cell tumor progression and metastasis through their interaction with key signaling pathways. However, their role in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains poorly understood, despite growing interest. In this study, we investigated SG formation and its regulatory effects on tumor progression and metastasis in OSCC. SG markers, including G3BP1, eIF2α, TIAR, and PABP, were significantly overexpressed in OSCC tissues compared with those in adjacent normal tissues. In mouse models established using OSCC cells subjected to hypoxia preconditioning or ISRIB treatment after sodium arsenite-induced stress, suppression of eIF2α phosphorylation was associated with reduced SG formation, tumor growth, and metastatic burden. Moreover, SG formation was elevated during hypoxia-induced stress, highlighting a stress-responsive regulatory mechanism. These findings indicate that SGs promote OSCC progression via eIF2α phosphorylation and might serve as a novel therapeutic target.

title: Metformin reverses lymphatic mitochondrial dysfunction induced by 5-FU chemotherapy
abstract: Abstract In western countries, secondary lymphedema often occurs after cancer treatments. However, lymphedema appears months, sometimes years after treatment suggesting that it is not only a side effect of surgery and may be promoted in part by cancer treatments. In this study, we demonstrate that the first line chemotherapeutic agent 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) induces lymphatic system damage, thereby increasing the risk of developing lymphedema. We found that metformin, a complex I respiration inhibitor widely used for decades in the treatment of diabetes, protects lymphatic endothelial cells and counteracts the deleterious effects of chemotherapy. Notably, metformin restores the gene expression of key molecules involved in lymphatic system maintenance, including Gata2, Foxc2, and Sox18. In vivo, the vessel collapse induced by 5-FU is not observed in the presence of metformin. In a murine model of lymphedema, metformin reduces the limb volume increased by 5-FU treatment. This is accompanied by a marked reduction in lymph reflux into tissues, a reduced dermal thickening, and disorganized lymphatic proliferation. Mechanistically, metformin prevents lymphatic endothelial cells from mitochondrial superoxide accumulation by restoring maximal respiration, ATP production, and spare respiratory capacity impaired by 5-FU, while also reducing mitochondrial mass. We found that the anti-oxidative effect of metformin is dependent on GATA2 pathway. Altogether, our study suggests that metformin could offer a pharmacological approach for the management of cancer-related secondary lymphedema.

title: Correction: RNA binding motif protein RBM41 promotes colorectal tumorigenesis by impeding the maturation of NDRG1 pre-mRNA
abstract: Since the online publication of this article, the authors have noticed that there was an error in Fig. 3. In the original version of this article, an error occurred during figure assembly. Due to a copy-paste mistake, the TUNEL staining image of the HT29 cell line with si RBM41 #1 in Figure 3D was inadvertently misplaced during figure assembly and upload, and the correct original image was not presented. The accurate Figure 3D has now been replaced, as shown in the Amended Figure 3.

title: Gut microbiota-derived 7-KDCA protects against diabetic sarcopenia by interrupting the NLRP1-ferroptosis crosstalk in myotubes
abstract: Abstract Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) accompanied by sarcopenia is an emerging clinical challenge in aging populations, yet the treatment options remain scarce. Recent advances in metabolomics have revealed that gut microbial bile acids function as essential players in muscle mass and function. The aim of the present study was to assess whether 7-ketodeoxycholic acid (7-KDCA), a secondary bile acid, can ameliorate muscle atrophy and physical exercise impairment in a diabetic mouse model of sarcopenia. Untargeted and targeted metabolomics showed that the fecal and serum levels of 7-KDCA were significantly downregulated in T2DM mice. This decrease was also observed in T2DM patients with sarcopenia, and the contents of 7-KDCA were positively associated with the skeletal muscle index (SMI) and skeletal muscle density (SMD) in enrolled patients. Administration of 7-KDCA ameliorated glucose intolerance, attenuated muscle atrophy, restored muscle function, enhanced exercise capacity, and improved intestinal permeability in T2DM mice. 7-KDCA facilitated the differentiation and protein synthesis, as well as glucose uptake, in cultured C2C12 myotubes. The abundance of Bifidobacterium pseudolongum ( B. pseudolongum ) and Lactobacillus murinus ( L. murinus ), two key bacteria for 7-KDCA production, was diminished in T2DM mice and patients. Intestinal colonization of B. pseudolongum and L. Murinus showed similar effects as 7-KDCA. RNA sequencing and experimental analysis revealed that 7-KDCA inhibited NLRP1 inflammasome activation to suppress ferroptosis in myotubes since a potent NLRP1 agonist, muramyl dipeptide (MDP), and a ferroptosis inducer, Erastin, minimized the benefits of 7-KDCA. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of 7-KDCA and its-generated B. pseudolongum and L. Murinus in alleviating diabetes-related muscle atrophy. Targeting 7-KDCA/NLRP1/ferroptosis axis offers a promising therapeutic strategy for metabolic disorders and sarcopenia.

title: Knockdown of lipocalin 2 alleviates ocular angiogenesis in diabetic retinopathy by lowering endothelial cell energy metabolism
abstract: Abstract Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is increasingly recognized as a neurovascular degenerative disease characterized by early neuronal dysfunction, chronic metabolic stress, and progressive microvascular abnormalities. Clinical studies have reported elevated levels of lipocalin-2 (LCN2) in patients with DR, however, the functional role of LCN2 in diabetic retinal vascular pathology remains poorly defined. In this study, we investigated the contribution of LCN2 to retinal vascular dysfunction under pathological conditions relevant to DR. Using an LCN2 overexpressing mouse model ( LCN2-Tg ) and an endothelium-specific LCN2 knockout mouse model ( Lcn2 fl/fl ; Cdh5-Cre ERT2 ), we examined the effects of LCN2 on retinal vascular remodeling and endothelial function. Our results showed that LCN2 deficiency suppressed both physiological and pathological retinal vascular expansion while preserving vascular stability. Mechanically, LCN2 overexpression was associated with enhanced endothelial cell energy metabolism and exacerbated pathological neovascularization, whereas downregulation of LCN2 suppressed endothelial cell proliferation and migration with restricted metabolic capacity. Collectively, our findings identify LCN2 as a regulator of endothelial metabolic competence in the diabetic retina and suggest that pathological upregulation of LCN2 contributes to retinal microvascular dysfunction. Targeting LCN2-dependent metabolic regulation may therefore represent a potential therapeutic strategy for diabetic retinopathy.

title: SRPX2 aggravates tumor progression and immune resistance through TGFBR2-mediated epithelial–mesenchymal transition in colorectal cancer
abstract: Abstract Colorectal cancer (CRC) metastasis presents a formidable clinical challenge, particularly for microsatellite stability (MSS) subtypes that show limited response to current targeted therapies and immunotherapies. While transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) signaling is recognized as an inducer of the mesenchymal transition program, including epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling in metastatic progression, the upstream molecular mechanisms controlling TGF-β pathway activation in metastasis remain unclear. Here, we identified sushi repeat-containing protein X-linked 2 (SRPX2) as a novel metastasis driver that orchestrates TGF-β signaling through an unexpected molecular mechanism. Our multi-omics analysis of metastatic CRC datasets revealed SRPX2 as the top candidate gene associated with aggressive progression and immunotherapy resistance. Mechanistically, SRPX2 binds to and stabilizes TGFBR2, activating the TGF-β signaling pathway that promotes EMT/ECM reprogramming. We further demonstrated that SRPX2 ablation suppresses liver metastasis and enhances tumor sensitivity to immune checkpoint inhibitors, accompanied by reduced mesenchymal abundance. These findings establish SRPX2 as a crucial molecular switch controlling TGF-β pathway activation in CRC metastasis and reveal its dual role in promoting stromal remodeling and immune evasion. Our work provides a compelling rationale for targeting the SRPX2/TGF-β axis as a novel therapeutic strategy for aggressive CRC subsets.

title: CXCR2 deficiency impairs auditory function in spiral ganglion neurons by altering excitability
abstract: Abstract CXC chemokine receptor 2 (CXCR2), a key member of the chemokine receptor family, plays a central role in regulating immune and inflammatory responses. Inflammation has been established as a critical pathological factor in various auditory disorders, including noise-induced hearing loss, drug-induced ototoxicity, and age-related hearing loss; however, the expression patterns and biological functions of CXCR2 in key cells involved in auditory signal transduction remain unclear. Here, we demonstrated that CXCR2 is abundantly expressed in cochlear spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs), hair cells, and the stria vascularis. Genetic deletion of CXCR2 resulted in progressive hearing loss in mice. SGNs from CXCR2 knockout mice exhibited increased expression of the Kv1.2 potassium channel, impaired ribbon synapses, and altered myelin integrity. Electrophysiological analysis revealed enhanced Kv1 currents and significantly reduced excitability in CXCR2-deficient SGNs. Notably, CXCR2 knockdown in SGNs using an adeno-associated virus recapitulated the hearing loss phenotype. In conclusion, our findings revealed that CXCR2 is essential for hearing as it regulates SGN excitability.

title: Targeting the AR-UBE2C axis unleashes autophagy-associated cell death to overcome intrinsic resistance to PI3K Inhibition in AR-overexpressed breast and prostate cancers
abstract: Abstract Luminal androgen receptor (LAR) subtype triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) overexpresses AR, making anti-androgen receptor therapy a viable strategy. The PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway is a critical driver of tumorigenesis, yet intrinsic resistance mechanisms often compromise the clinical efficacy of PI3K inhibitors. In this study, we identified a novel isoflavone fluorinated derivative, compound 8, as a potential PI3K inhibitor. While compound 8 exhibited robust anti-tumor activity in AR-low triple-negative breast cancer cells (MDA-MB-231), AR-high cells (MDA-MB-453) displayed significant resistance. We demonstrated that high AR abundance blocks drug-induced autophagy-associated cell death and cell cycle arrest. Transcriptomic and functional analyses revealed that AR confers resistance by upregulating UBE2C. High levels of UBE2C not only sustained mitotic progression but also maintained autophagy inhibition, thereby limiting compound 8-induced autophagy-associated cytotoxicity. Importantly, we validated the universality of this mechanism in prostate cancer models using AR-high LNCaP cells and AR-low PC-3 cells. Genetic silencing of AR or pharmacological inhibition with Enz sensitized resistant cells to compound 8, enhancing cell-cycle arrest and promoting autophagy-associated cytotoxicity. Furthermore, the combination therapy synergistically suppressed tumor growth and metastasis in vivo. Collectively, our findings identify a novel PI3K inhibitor with potent inhibitory activity against both AR-low breast and prostate cancers, as well as elucidate a conserved AR-UBE2C-PI3K resistance axis across breast and prostate cancers, providing compelling preclinical rationale for combining PI3K inhibitors with anti-androgen therapy to overcome drug resistance.

title: Inhibition of cGAS-STING signaling and NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis reduces lens opacity and inflammation in high glucose-induced cataract
abstract: Abstract Diabetic cataract (DC) is a major cause of visual impairment among diabetic individuals, involving significant inflammatory injury to lens epithelial cells (LECs). However, mechanisms linking high glucose (HG) conditions to inflammatory cell death in LECs remain incompletely understood. This study investigated the role of cytosolic DNA-sensing cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling in promoting NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome activation and pyroptosis-associated injury in DC. We found that cGAS, STING, NLRP3, caspase-1, and gasdermin D (GSDMD) were significantly upregulated in LECs from human DC anterior lens capsules. In vitro, HG exposure induced cytosolic DNA accumulation, mitochondrial DNA release and cGAS-STING signaling activation in human LECs, accompanied by upregulation of NLRP3 inflammasome, ASC, cleavage of caspase-1 and GSDMD, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release, and elevated secretion of interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and IL-18. Knocking down NLRP3 with small interfering RNA (siRNA) effectively attenuated pyroptosis-associated responses of LECs under HG, with decrease of ASC, cleaved caspase-1, cleaved GSDMD, LDH release, and secretion of IL-1β and IL-18. Furthermore, knockdown of cGAS or STING suppressed activation of the NLRP3-caspase-1-GSDMD axis, suggesting cGAS-STING signaling may contribute to the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and pyroptosis-associated injury. In diabetic rat model, therapeutic intervention with siRNAs targeting cGAS, STING, or NLRP3 significantly attenuated lens opacity and effectively improved histopathological alterations in the lens epithelium and cortex. Collectively, these findings indicate that HG promotes cytosolic DNA accumulation, and the cGAS-STING and NLRP3 signaling may represent a potentially important inflammatory pathway involved in pyroptosis-associated injury in DC. Inhibition of the cGAS-STING signaling or NLRP3 inflammasome may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for DC.

title: Transglutaminase 2 contributes to the blood clotting cascade
abstract: Abstract Cross-linking of fibrin and associated proteins via Nε-(γ-glutamyl)lysine bonds in clot formation is a well-established component of the hemodynamic mechanism, providing clot rigidity and reducing the rate of fibrinolysis. The latter effect occurs predominantly through the incorporation of fibrinolytic inhibitors. To date, this function has been attributed exclusively to Factor XIIIa, also known as plasma transglutaminase (TG), one of eight identified in mammals. In this report, we demonstrate that tissue transglutaminase (TG2), a ubiquitous enzyme abundantly present in erythrocytes, also contributed to clot stabilisation. We observed clear differences between whole thrombi isolated from TG2-deficient and wild-type mice. Similarly, human thrombi were more stable in the presence of TG2 than when TG2 activity is specifically inhibited, revealing a previously unrecognized role for this enzyme in haemostasis. Therefore, we propose TG2 as an additional factor involved in blood coagulation.

title: Long non-coding RNA NEAT1 drives nuclear condensates regulating gene expression and ferroptosis vulnerability in pancreatic cancer cells
abstract: Abstract Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive malignancy with poor patient outcomes due to development of tumor cell drug resistance impacting treatment efficacy. Shifts in tumor cell transcriptional subtypes from well-differentiated classical to poorly differentiated basal-like cells can drive PDAC chemotherapeutic resistance. Such transcriptomic changes have been linked to cellular metabolic states, but how coordination of transcriptional and metabolic programs is mediated at the molecular level remains unclear. The stress-responsive long noncoding RNA NEAT1 , an essential constituent of nuclear condensates called paraspeckles, has been associated with classical PDAC and was previously linked to regulation of cellular metabolism. In this study, we utilized a high-throughput drug screening approach in NEAT1 -deficient cancer cells to uncover functional metabolic targets in these cells, identifying ferroptosis via GPX4 inhibition as a major vulnerability of cells lacking paraspeckles. We find that the paraspeckle-forming isoform of NEAT1 is central to ferroptosis suppression, and we extend these results into PDAC cell line models with genetic suppression or activation of NEAT1 . We find that NEAT1 -nucleated paraspeckles underlie the expression program tied to the classical PDAC subtype and promote ferroptosis resistance. We pinpoint the paraspeckle-suppressive RNA-binding protein QKI, associated with basal-like PDAC, as a positive regulator of ferroptosis susceptibility, possibly through its suppression of paraspeckles. These results link NEAT1 and regulation of paraspeckle condensates to subtype-specific ferroptosis susceptibility in PDAC and offer novel avenues for targeting metabolic vulnerabilities of pancreatic cancer cells on the basis of transcriptional subtype.

title: Mppa sustains cyst stem cell maintenance and orchestrates germ cell differentiation through nonautonomous regulation of mitochondrial homeostasis in Drosophila testes
abstract: Abstract The intricate balance maintaining CySCs and facilitating their differentiation within the testicular stem cell niche remains a complex process. However, the mechanisms underlying CySC maintenance and their nonautonomous impact on GSC differentiation and downstream effects remain elusive. This study elucidates the pivotal role of Mppa in orchestrating the stem cell niche and germ cell differentiation in Drosophila testes. Through targeted manipulation of Mppa levels in the CySC lineage, we uncovered CySC maintenance and germ cell differentiation defects. We further discovered Mppa as a conserved mitochondrial protein crucial for maintaining ATP homeostasis. Transcriptomic analysis revealed Mppa’s influence on mitochondrial function, particularly through pathways involving cytochrome P450. Furthermore, our exploration of Mppa-binding proteins via LC–MS/MS identified associations with diverse energy metabolism processes, oxidation–reduction reactions, and cellular redox balance, with specific interactions validated, such as UQCR-C1. This comprehensive investigation unveils Mppa’s pivotal function in governing nonautonomous germ cell differentiation through energy equilibrium in Drosophila testes, providing novel insights into spermatogenesis disorders linked to disrupted germ cell differentiation. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: Amyloid β peptides alter redox status and oxygen transport function of red blood cells
abstract: Abstract Patients with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) exhibit reduced cerebral venous oxygen saturation, that progresses with disease severity and correlates with cognitive decline. The underlying causes of this hypoxia, however, remain unclear. The accumulation of beta-amyloid (Aβ 42 ) and its pathological isoform with isomerized Asp7 (isoAβ 42 ) in the brain are the key pathological factors in AD. Given that red blood cells (RBCs) are the primary carrier of Aβ in the bloodstream and their loading with Aβ 42 increases with age and AD, we studied whether Aβ 42 and isoAβ 42 binding affects human RBC oxygen transport. Here, we demonstrate for the first time that elevated beta-amyloids binding to RBCs reduces hemoglobin oxygen affinity and slows down the rate of oxygen release. This reduction of hemoglobin oxygen affinity is caused by a decrease in the level of reactive oxygen species (ROS). As a result, Aβ 42 binding decreases hemoglobin glutathionylation and its alpha-helical content, whereas isoAβ 42 reduces NO level and alters heme-state of hemoglobin. Importantly, inhibition of NADPH oxidase abolishes the impact of Aβ on ROS, oxygen affinity and alpha-helical content. Therefore, we propose that beta-amyloids impair erythrocyte oxygen affinity primarily through the suppression of NADPH oxidase activity. Moreover, we found a negative correlation between the Aβ 42 amount on the surface of RBCs and the level of intracellular ROS in transgenic APP/PS1-mouse model of AD. The study reveals a new role for Aβ 42 in the regulation of Hb-O₂-affinity and O₂-release from RBCs, raising the possibility of one mechanism underlying the reduced blood oxygen saturation reported in Alzheimer’s disease.

title: Hydrogen sulfide promotes S-sulfhydration of TrxR1 and attenuates diabetic vascular remodeling
abstract: Abstract Diabetic vasculopathy represents one of the most serious complications of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Growing evidence suggests that its pathogenesis is closely linked to chronic inflammation-driven phenotypic switching of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), which under hyperglycemic conditions exhibit heightened proliferative and migratory activity. While hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) is known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory roles in diabetic vasculopathy, the specific mechanisms by which H₂S alleviates these abnormal VSMCs phenotypes in T2DM remain unclear. Using T2DM mice and mouse aortic vascular smooth muscle cells (MOVAS) cultured under high-glucose-high-fat (HGHF) conditions, we observed a marked decrease in both the expression of the H₂S-synthesizing enzyme cystathionine γ-lyase (CSE) and endogenous H₂S production. These changes were accompanied by elevated oxidative stress, activation of the NOD-like receptor pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome, and enhanced MOVAS proliferation and migration. Notably, the H₂S donor NaHS reversed these changes. Further investigation into protein S-sulfhydration revealed that H₂S promotes the S-sulfhydration of thioredoxin reductase 1 (TrxR1). Through pharmacological inhibition and rescue experiments, we demonstrated that H₂S mediates S-sulfhydration at the Cys611 residue of TrxR1, thereby regulating its enzymatic activity and influencing the thioredoxin 1 (Trx1)–thioredoxin-interacting protein (TXNIP)–NLRP3 signaling axis. This process leads to suppression of inflammasome activation and contributes to the antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-migratory, and anti-proliferative effects observed in MOVAS. Our study reveals a novel pathway whereby H₂S alleviates diabetic vascular complications via TrxR1 S-sulfhydration at Cys611 and subsequent inhibition of the Trx1–TXNIP–NLRP3 axis, highlighting a promising therapeutic target.

title: FBXO28 promotes the malignancy of non-small cell lung cancer through ubiquitination-mediated activation of BRD4
abstract: Abstract The E3 ubiquitin ligase FBXO28 has been implicated in the progression of various cancers, yet its precise function and substrates remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the role of FBXO28 in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and its underlying mechanism. We observed an upregulation of FBXO28 in NSCLC, and higher FBXO28 levels correlated with poorer patient outcomes. Functional experiments revealed that silencing FBXO28 inhibited NSCLC proliferation, migration, and invasion and induced apoptosis, whereas overexpressing FBXO28 had the opposite effects. Using coimmunoprecipitation (co-IP) assays, we identified an interaction between FBXO28 and BRD4. Further investigations revealed that FBXO28 mediated the ubiquitination of BRD4 at K395 through a K63-conjugated model. The ubiquitination by FBXO28 does not lead to the degradation of BRD4, but promotes its transcriptional coactivation, as the modulation of FBXO28 affects the expression of BRD4-targeting genes and the binding of BRD4 to the promoters of its target genes. Mechanistically, FBXO28-mediated ubiquitination of BRD4 facilitates the activation of P-TEFb and subsequent phosphorylation of the serine 2 (Ser2) C-terminal domain (CTD) of the largest subunit of RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) to initiate transcription. Furthermore, in a positive feedback loop, BRD4 binds to the FBXO28 promoter and increased FBXO28 transcription. In summary, our findings highlight the pivotal role of the FBXO28/BRD4 positive feedback loop in driving the malignancy of NSCLC.

title: UVB-induced keratinocyte disulfidptosis drives skin photodamage and photoaging
abstract: Abstract Environmental stressors challenge cellular homeostasis, yet how they corrupt proteostasis to drive tissue injury remains incompletely defined. Here, we report that aberrant accumulation of disulfide-crosslinked proteins, a hallmark of disulfide stress, acts as a novel, actionable molecular lesion in ultraviolet B (UVB)-induced skin photodamage and photoaging. This lesion executes disulfidptosis, a recently discovered form of regulated cell death. We demonstrate that disulfide stress acts as a quantifiable pathogenic continuum, linking acute UVB insult to chronic tissue degeneration in skin. Core biochemical features of disulfidptosis, including NADPH depletion, excessive disulfide-bond formation, and F-actin collapse, were consistently observed in human keratinocytes from physiologically relevant systems: sun-exposed skin, ex vivo UVB-irradiated skin, and keratinocytes cultured in vitro. Genetic and pharmacological interrogation across murine models of chronic and acute injury established NCKAP1 as an essential mediator and revealed that inhibition of this pathway (via the reducing agent TCEP) robustly mitigates keratinocyte death and tissue damage. Our work defines UVB-induced disulfide stress and NCKAP1-mediated disulfidptosis as a previously unrecognized proteotoxic axis in environmental skin disease. We posit that disulfide-bond dyshomeostasis may represent a targetable vulnerability in a range of age-related and environmental pathologies characterized by proteostasis collapse, offering a new paradigm for therapeutic intervention beyond dermatology.

title: PLA2G4A-driven arachidonic acid metabolic reprogramming promotes NSCLC progression via the HSF1 signaling axis
abstract: Abstract Aberrant arachidonic acid (AA) metabolism is a hallmark of cancer, and cytosolic phospholipase A2 (PLA2G4A) is the rate-limiting enzyme that initiates this cascade. However, the cell-intrinsic role of PLA2G4A and its downstream signaling mechanisms in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remain poorly understood. Here, we show that PLA2G4A is significantly upregulated in NSCLC patients and cell lines. Gain-of-function experiments in 16HBE normal bronchial epithelial cells demonstrate that ectopic PLA2G4A expression promotes proliferation, induces epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and cooperates with MYC to drive tumor formation in vivo. Conversely, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated knockout of PLA2G4A suppresses cell proliferation, soft agar colony formation, and invasion, while inducing G1 phase arrest and apoptosis. In vivo, PLA2G4A knockout inhibits tumor growth and lung colonization. Mechanistically, transcriptomics and biochemical analysis reveal that PLA2G4A knockout reduces IL-1β expression and suppresses MAPK pathway activity, leading to decreased phosphorylation of heat shock factor 1 (HSF1). Pharmacological inhibition of IL-1β phenocopies these effects, and ectopic HSF1 expression rescues the proliferative defect caused by PLA2G4A ablation. Upstream, we identify SP1 as a candidate transcriptional regulator of PLA2G4A. Collectively, these findings suggest a linear SP1/PLA2G4A/IL-1β/MAPK/HSF1 signaling axis that operates cell-intrinsically to promote NSCLC proliferation, survival, and metastasis. Targeting this pathway may represent a potential therapeutic avenue for NSCLC.

title: Targeting NAT10 alleviates granulosa cells oxidative stress and follicular atresia by disrupting ac4C acetylation of Tnc
abstract: Abstract Follicular atresia mediated by programmed granulosa cells (GCs) death directly contributes to ovarian dysfunction-related disorders and infertility or subfertility in mammals. N-acetyltransferase 10 (NAT10)-catalyzed N4-acetylcytidine (ac4C) modification has been identified to drive multiple biological processes, but its function in GCs death and follicular atresia is unclear. In this study, we found that a significant increase in both the ac4C RNA level and NAT10 expression in atretic follicle. Functionally, NAT10 promotes oxidative stress by inhibiting the mitophagy of GCs in vitro. Mechanistically, we identified Tnc mRNA, an important extracellular matrix glycoprotein, as a direct target of NAT10-catalyzed ac4C modification. This modification enhances the mRNA stability of Tnc, inhibits the mitophagy and promotes the oxidative stress of GCs, thereby contributing to follicular atresia progression. Additionally, we revealed that Tnc directly binds with Parkin and accelerates the ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of Parkin, leading to inhibition of Parkin-mediated mitophagy pathway. Notably, Remodelin, a specific NAT10 inhibitor, promotes the mitophagy and inhibits the oxidative stress of GCs in vitro, and hinders follicular atresia and ameliorates impaired reproductive efficiency caused by oxidative stress of GCs in vivo through NAT10-ac4C-Tnc pathway. These findings suggested that NAT10 drives follicular atresia progression via Tnc mRNA stability regulation, and Remodelin could be a promising therapeutic candidate for targeting NAT10 in follicular atresia and infertility or subfertility treatment.

title: Exosome-induced ferroptosis mediates cochlear hair cell injury via GPX4 suppression and iron overload
abstract: Abstract Vestibular schwannoma (VS) is the most common benign tumor in the cerebellopontine angle, with approximately 95% of patients suffering sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL). Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by lipid peroxidation, has been implicated in cochlear hair cell vulnerability. However, its role in VS-associated SNHL remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated whether VS-derived exosomes (VS-Exos) contribute to SNHL by inducing ferroptosis in cochlear hair cells. Proteomic and bioinformatic analyses were performed to compare exosomes from VS patients with poor hearing (PH-Exos) versus those with good hearing (GH-Exos). In vitro and in vivo experiments were conducted to assess the damaging effects of VS-Exos on cochlear hair cells and to evaluate the protective effect of the ferroptosis inhibitor ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1). Our results demonstrate that VS-Exos promote ferroptosis in cochlear hair cells by downregulating glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and disrupting iron homeostasis, leading to accumulation of ferrous ions, reactive oxygen species, and lipid peroxidation. Notably, PH-Exos induced significantly greater ferroptotic damage than GH-Exos. Treatment with Fer-1 effectively alleviated hair cell injury and preserved auditory function in vivo. These findings uncover a novel mechanism by which VS-Exos contribute to hearing loss through GPX4 suppression and iron dyshomeostasis, and suggest that targeting ferroptosis or exosome-mediated signaling may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for hearing preservation in VS.

title: Histone lactylation mediates the regulation of dental follicle cells' senescence driven by RUNX2 during the process of tooth eruption
abstract: Abstract Cleidocranial dysplasia (CCD), an autosomal dominant disorder caused by RUNX2 mutation, is characterized by delayed or failed eruption of the permanent teeth; however, the pathogenesis of tooth impaction remains unclear. Tooth eruption is a complex developmental process in which the dental follicle plays a crucial role. Although the dental follicle is known to coordinate osteoclastogenesis and osteogenesis, the precise cellular mechanisms that initiate eruption are still not fully defined. Moreover, how dental follicles activate the signals of tooth eruption and whether the other biological alterations occur in CCD dental follicles have not been reported. Previous work from our group demonstrated that RUNX2 mutations inhibit dental follicle cell senescence in CCD patients. Cellular senescence participates in diverse physiological and pathological processes and is increasingly implicated as a dynamic regulator of morphogenesis and tissue remodeling. This study investigates whether the senescence of dental follicle cells (DFCs) critically mediates tooth eruption and elucidates its underlying regulatory mechanism. Analysis of dental follicle tissues showed a significant reduction in SA-β-gal-positive and P16 INK4a -positive cells in CCD patients compared with healthy controls. Animal studies revealed a progressive accumulation of senescent cells in the dental follicle during normal tooth eruption, whereas this accumulation was suppressed in Runx2 +/− mice, which exhibit delayed tooth eruption. Inhibition of dental follicle senescence via nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) in wild-type mice similarly delayed tooth eruption, confirming the functional necessity of DFCs senescence. Mechanistically, RUNX2 knockdown or mutation upregulated HDAC3 expression, which catalyzed histone delactylation, predominantly at H3K18. The reduced H3K18la levels could lead to transcriptional repression of PLAU. Thus, RUNX2 knockdown or mutation suppressed DFCs senescence via the HDAC3/H3K18la/PLAU axis. Collectively, our study reveals that DFCs senescence acts as an important driver of tooth eruption and identifies a novel epigenetic regulatory mechanism involving histone lactylation that regulates cellular senescence mediated by RUNX2.

title: Regulatory T cell instability facilitates blood–brain barrier disruption via the β-catenin-tight junctions axis, leading to perioperative neurocognitive disorders
abstract: Abstract Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND) are significant neurological complications in elderly surgical patients, yet the underlying immune-mediated mechanisms remain elusive. Blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption is increasingly recognized as a critical neurovascular event in PND and may result from perioperative immune dysregulation. Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are key mediators of neurovascular homeostasis and BBB integrity. We therefore investigated whether perioperative Treg instability contributed to BBB disruption and PND. Single-cell transcriptomic profiling of perioperative PBMCs from elderly surgical patients revealed marked remodeling of the CD4 + T-cell compartment, characterized by disproportionate loss of Tregs and functional destabilization. Tregs shifted from resting and immunosuppressive states toward an inflammatory-shifted state, accompanied by reduced expression of regulatory and tissue-reparative genes, including FOXP3 , CTLA4 , PDCD1 , and AREG . Comparative transcriptomic analysis of Tregs identified 34 dexmedetomidine-corrected genes, with CTNNB1 , encoding β-catenin, emerging as a prominent candidate hub within the protein–protein interaction network. These findings support β-catenin-associated signaling as an important regulatory pathway involved in perioperative Treg destabilization. Mouse hippocampal scRNA-seq revealed postoperative endothelial remodeling characterized by reduced S1pr1 and Cldn5 and increased Icam1 expression. In a murine PND model, β-catenin activation restored postoperative Treg abundance and regulatory gene expression while preserving hippocampal endothelial barrier programs, as evidenced by increased S1PR1 and Claudin-5 and reduced ICAM1 expression. These protective effects were markedly attenuated by PC61-mediated depletion of the Treg compartment, supporting an important Treg-dependent contribution. Furthermore, recombinant PD-L1-Fc treatment restored postoperative Treg abundance and was associated with preserved ultrastructural BBB integrity, reduced Evans blue-defined BBB leakage, attenuated hippocampal neuroinflammation, and improved cognitive function. These findings identify perioperative Treg instability as a prominent immune-associated contributor to BBB disruption and cognitive dysfunction. They further position Treg-associated β-catenin signaling as an important regulatory pathway contributing to the maintenance of neurovascular integrity.

title: Targeting CD44v6 and PI3K disrupts HGF-driven reprogramming of colorectal cancer stem cells
abstract: Abstract Therapeutic adaptive responses and secondary resistance represent major obstacles to effective colorectal cancer treatment. These dynamic adaptations arise within a permissive tumor microenvironment that sustains cancer cell survival, epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity and the outgrowth of drug-tolerant clones, ultimately driving disease progression and poor patient outcomes. Here, it is shown that AMC303, a highly selective CD44v6 inhibitor, needs to be combined with a PI3K/mTOR inhibitor to prevent or reverse anti-tumor therapeutic resistance and disease progression under tumor microenvironmental cues. Cytokines released by tumor-associated cells, such as HGF, induce c-Met phosphorylation, CD44v6 expression and enhanced clonogenicity, thereby expanding cancer stem cell populations that undergo transcriptional reprogramming towards a hybrid EMT state with increased resistance and metastatic potential. In colorectal cancer stem cell mouse avatars, HGF promotes phenotypic reprogramming even when canonical CD44v6/c-Met signaling is blocked by AMC303, acting instead through c-Met co-receptors and downstream PI3K/AKT and MAPK pathways. By suppressing compensatory PI3K/AKT and MAPK signaling, the addition of Apitolisib, the dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitor, reduces the proliferation rate and makes cancer cells more vulnerable to the in vitro exposure with standard chemotherapeutic regimen. Collectively, these findings support a therapeutic strategy that targets key molecular mechanisms underlying cancer cell reprogramming, adaptive therapeutic escape and the emergence of aggressive colorectal cancer phenotypes.

title: MAIT cells protect against alcohol-associated liver injury via an IL-10–macrophage–CXCL1 axis
abstract: Abstract Mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells are enriched in the liver and contribute to immune regulation, but their role in alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD), particularly in neutrophil-driven inflammation, remains unclear. We examined MAIT cell frequency and function in blood from ALD patients and in the liver, spleen, and peripheral blood from ethanol-fed mice, and used wild-type and MR1-deficient (MR1 −/− ) mice exposed to chronic-binge and acute ethanol, with 5-OP-RU, recombinant IL-10, or a CXCL1-neutralizing antibody as interventions. MAIT cells were reduced in ALD patients and ethanol-fed mice, and showed an activated but functionally impaired phenotype. MAIT cell deficiency aggravated ethanol-induced liver injury, steatosis, oxidative stress, and inflammation, whereas 5-OP-RU–mediated expansion was protective. RNA-seq and flow cytometric analyses revealed that MAIT cell deficiency was associated with increased accumulation of monocyte-derived macrophages (MoMFs) and enhanced CD86 expression, whereas Kupffer cells (KCs) showed no significant phenotypic changes. MAIT cells preferentially regulated MoMFs rather than hepatocytes, thereby restraining CXCL1 production and hepatic neutrophil recruitment. Mechanistically, this regulation depended on MAIT-derived IL-10, as either IL-10 administration or CXCL1 blockade attenuated liver injury in ethanol-fed MR1 −/− mice. Overall, our data define a MAIT–IL-10–macrophage–CXCL1 axis that restrains neutrophil-driven inflammation in ALD and represents a regulatory checkpoint in disease progression.

title: Differential redox-mitochondrial adaptation to ultra-high-dose-rate irradiation in astrocytes and glioma cells
abstract: Abstract FLASH radiotherapy (FLASH-RT) delivers radiation at ultra-high dose rates (UHDRs) and has been reported to reduce normal tissue toxicity while maintaining tumor control, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying the ‘FLASH effect’ remain incompletely defined. FLASH-RT has been associated with differential normal and tumor tissue responses in preclinical studies, although the early cellular processes induced under these conditions remain incompletely understood. Here, we compared FLASH-RT versus conventional radiotherapy (CONV-RT) in murine glioma GL261 cells and primary healthy astrocytic cultures, focusing on redox dynamics, mitochondrial function, bioenergetics, and transcriptional stress programs. Using real-time kinetic assays, flow cytometry, Seahorse analysis, and gene expression profiling, we found that in healthy astrocytes FLASH-RT reduced acute ROS accumulation, limited cell death, and was associated with greater preservation of mitochondrial membrane potential and respiratory capacity compared with CONV-RT. FLASH-RT was also associated with sustained induction of cell-cycle checkpoint and senescence-associated transcripts. In GL261 cells, FLASH-RT produced a lower initial ROS peak followed by continued ROS accumulation over time and enhanced G2/M accumulation, together with persistent mitochondrial depolarization and respiratory suppression. Annexin V analysis at 8 Gy revealed comparable levels of Annexin V positivity between FLASH- and CONV-RT, whereas FLASH-treated cells showed greater G2/M accumulation and metabolic dysfunction, consistent with altered cell-cycle progression rather than enhanced Annexin V-defined cell death. Pharmacological modulation with DPQ, Calpeptin, Nec-1 and zVAD differentially affected mitochondrial bioenergetic parameters across irradiation modalities and cell types, providing functional evidence for the potential contribution of distinct stress- and cell-death-associated signaling pathways to radiation-induced metabolic dysfunction. Similar stress responses were also observed in human U87 glioblastoma cells, where FLASH-RT induced stronger ROS accumulation, greater Annexin V positivity, and alterations in NAD⁺ levels associated with mitochondrial respiratory impairment compared with CONV-RT. Collectively, these data indicate that FLASH-RT elicits cell-type-specific redox–mitochondrial responses associated with relative preservation of mitochondrial function in healthy astrocytes and prolonged metabolic stress and altered cell-cycle dynamics in glioma cells, highlighting distinct early adaptations to FLASH irradiation in astrocytic and glioma models.

title: 4-Octyl itaconate promotes dendritic cell tolerogenic properties via suppressing STING signaling to delay lupus onset
abstract: Abstract Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a refractory autoimmune disease characterized by immune tolerance breakdown and dendritic cell (DCs) hyperactivation. Tolerogenic DCs (tolDCs) represent a promising therapeutic strategy, yet the regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the therapeutic potential and mechanism of the 4-octyl itaconate (4OI) and 4OI-induced tolDCs in SLE. In a chromatin-induced murine lupus model, 4OI administration significantly delayed disease onset, reduced proteinuria, anti-dsDNA autoantibodies, and renal pathological injury. Mechanistically, 4OI directly promoted a tolDCs phenotype both in vivo and in vitro, as evidenced by downregulated CD80/CD86, upregulated PD-L1, increased IL-10/TGF-β, and impaired CD4⁺ T cell proliferation. Adoptive transfer of 4OI-induced tolDCs alleviated lupus progression, reducing Tfh, Th1, Th17, and plasma cells while increasing Tregs. Further investigation showed that 4OI promotes tolDCs differentiation by reducing STING mRNA stability and inhibiting its phosphorylation. Notably, combining 4OI with the JAK inhibitor produced synergistic therapeutic effects superior to either monotherapy. These findings identify a previously unrecognized role of itaconate derivatives in promoting tolDCs via STING inhibition and suggest that 4OI and 4OI-induced tolDCs represents an attractive candidate for SLE therapy.

title: Selective integration of transplanted mitochondria drive sustained metabolic and functional rescue in MELAS endothelial cells through enhanced protein translation
abstract: Abstract Mitochondrial diseases such as mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes (MELAS) manifest due to mutations in the mitochondrial genome. This leads to defects in mitochondrial respiration and ATP generation, affecting normal cellular function. Recently, it has been shown that the transfer of healthy donor mitochondria into recipient cells, termed “mitotherapy”, has been successful in boosting recipient cell metabolism and function. However, the mechanistic route by which mitotherapy promotes cellular function is uncertain. Here we demonstrate in vitro uptake of exogenous donor mitochondria and expression of the donor mitochondrial genes, resulting in metabolic and functional improvements in MELAS endothelial cells. Improvements were evident at both early and prolonged time points following treatment using healthy, functioning mitochondria, in contrast to the treatment of MELAS mutant mitochondria or sonicated healthy mitochondria. Transcriptomic analysis suggests that the improved cellular energetics enabled an upregulation of translation machinery, potentially counteracting the translational deficiencies characteristic of MELAS. Importantly, the treated healthy wild-type mitochondria are retained in recipient MELAS endothelial cells, decreasing their mutant mitochondrial DNA load, termed heteroplasmy. These findings suggest a novel route in tackling diseases that stem from mitochondrial dysfunctions.

title: MTRF1 reverses cisplatin resistance in bladder cancer by competitively disrupting OTUB1-mediated deubiquitination of SLC25A5 to trigger ferroptosis
abstract: Abstract Cisplatin (DDP)-based chemotherapy remains a standard treatment for advanced bladder cancer, yet acquired resistance remains a major cause of therapeutic failure. Here, we identify mitochondrial translation release factor 1 (MTRF1) as a critical suppressor of cisplatin resistance and a regulator of ferroptotic vulnerability in bladder cancer. MTRF1 was markedly downregulated in bladder cancer tissues and was further reduced in cisplatin-resistant clinical specimens as well as in T24-DDP and 5637-DDP resistant cell models. Restoration of MTRF1 significantly resensitized resistant cells to cisplatin, decreased IC50 values, and suppressed proliferation, colony formation, migration, and survival. Mechanistically, MTRF1 promoted a ferroptosis-prone state, as evidenced by elevated intracellular iron and malondialdehyde, increased Acyl-CoA Synthetase Long Chain Family Member 4 (ACSL4), reduced Glutathione Peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and Solute Carrier Family 7 Member 11 (SLC7A11), and enhanced sensitivity to Erastin. MTRF1 also triggered mitochondrial membrane depolarization, reactive oxygen species accumulation, oxidative redox shift, a reduced GSH/GSSG ratio, and inhibition of the Nrf2/HO-1 antioxidant program, indicating a profound collapse of mitochondrial and redox homeostasis. At the molecular level, MTRF1 physically interacted with Solute Carrier Family 25 Member 5 (SLC25A5) and antagonized its pro-survival function. Further analyses demonstrated that MTRF1 promoted ubiquitin-proteasome-mediated degradation of SLC25A5 by increasing its polyubiquitination and competitively displacing the deubiquitinase OTUB1. In vivo, MTRF1 restoration enhanced cisplatin responsiveness in xenograft models, whereas deferoxamine partially reversed the antitumor effect, supporting a partial contribution of ferroptosis to this response. Collectively, these findings establish MTRF1 as a key determinant of cisplatin sensitivity in bladder cancer and uncover an MTRF1-OTUB1-SLC25A5 axis that links mitochondrial proteostasis to oxidative stress and ferroptotic cell death. Targeting this pathway may represent a promising strategy for overcoming cisplatin resistance in bladder cancer.

title: USP24 and NF-κB formed a positive regulatory loop increases BMP4 to induce cardiac fibrosis during lung cancer progression
abstract: Abstract Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) and cancer are the leading causes of death worldwide each year. This study showed that EGFR L858R -induced lung cancer mice exhibited reduced heart function, which could be improved by knocking out USP24 or treating with a specific USP24 inhibitor, USP24-i-101. Bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4), a member of the TGF-β superfamily, in cancer cells and M2 macrophages, is inhibited by USP24-i-101 or by silencing USP24. NF-κB can be recruited to the promoter of BMP4 to enhance its transcription activity. There is a positive feedback regulation between USP24 and NF-κB, increasing transcriptional activity to induce BMP4 expression in cancer cells and M2 macrophages. Secreted BMP4 from macrophages and cancer cells activates the SMAD pathway in cardiomyocytes, inducing fibrosis-related gene expression. In cardiac myoblasts, H9c2 cells, USP24 is also positively feedback regulated with BRD7 to activate the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, thereby inducing fibrosis-related gene expression. In summary, the positive feedback regulation between USP24 and NF-κB in lung cancer cells and M2 macrophages enhances BMP4 expression, causing fibrosis of cardiac myoblasts. Additionally, the positive feedback regulation between USP24 and BRD7 in cardiac myocytes activates the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, leading to fibrosis of myoblasts. Targeting USP24 with USP24-i-101 in lung cancer patients may improve cardiac activity by inhibiting heart tissue fibrosis.

title: A lncRNA–miRNA axis regulates the balance between proliferative and invasive states in melanoma
abstract: Abstract Melanoma is a highly aggressive malignancy characterized by significant phenotypic plasticity, allowing tumor cells to transit between different phenotypic states. This process, known as phenotype switching, drives metastasis and therapeutic resistance. While the primary transcriptional markers defining these states are well-established, the non-coding regulatory networks that stabilize these phenotypes remain incompletely understood. In this study, we identify the long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) LINC00504 and LINC00520 as key components of a multilayered regulatory circuit associated with the regulation of the proliferative/invasive melanoma subtypes. Functional assays reveal that experimental silencing of LINC00504 or LINC00520 in proliferative cells is sufficient to enhance the migratory and invasive capacity of melanoma cells, effectively mimicking the phenotype switch toward the invasive state. Mechanistically, these lncRNAs function as competing endogenous RNAs (ceRNAs) in the cytoplasm, where they sequester specific microRNAs to prevent the repression of mRNA targets, including MITF . Furthermore, we establish that MITF directly binds to the regulatory elements of both lncRNAs to drive their transcription, forming a positive feedback loop that reinforces the proliferative transcriptional program. Disruption of this MITF-lncRNA-miRNA axis facilitates the transition toward an invasive phenotype. Collectively, our findings highlight a novel integrated regulatory circuit that maintains melanoma cell state stability and suggest that targeting these non-coding components may provide a strategy to overcome phenotypic plasticity and therapeutic adaptability in melanoma.

title: Colon cancer cells survive and recover proliferation under prolonged glucose deprivation
abstract: Abstract Metabolic plasticity enables cancer cells to survive fluctuations in nutrient availability within the tumor microenvironment. Although most colorectal cancer (CRC) cells are highly dependent on glucose-driven glycolysis, we demonstrate that CRC cells can survive prolonged glucose deprivation and can establish a glucose deprivation-resistant (GDR) state characterized by sustained restoration of proliferation in the absence of glucose in the medium. Upon complete glucose deprivation, a fraction of cells dies, whereas the remaining population enters a senescence-like dormant state (Dorm) marked by growth arrest, elevated ROS, urea-cycle-associated metabolic remodeling, and accumulation of DNA damage. After approximately one month, a subset of these dormant cells acquires glucose-deprivation resistance and resumes proliferation in glucose-free medium. In the GDR state, cells maintain oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) while establishing enhanced redox control associated with one-carbon, transsulfuration, and glutathione metabolism and reduced DNA-damage signaling. Functional perturbation of redox control, mitochondrial fatty-acid utilization, and PERK/ISR stress-response signaling impaired cell survival and/or long-term proliferative capacity, whereas antioxidant supplementation facilitated proliferative recovery of Dorm cells. GDR populations additionally underwent pronounced oligoclonal expansion during acquisition of the GDR phenotype. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that colorectal cancer cells can adapt to prolonged glucose deprivation by establishing a distinct metabolic and stress-adapted state oriented toward OXPHOS, redox control, and sustained proliferation.

title: Discovery of the antifungal butoconazole as a potent inhibitor of energy metabolism that drives liver cancer cell death via autophagy impairment
abstract: Abstract Metabolic plasticity is a hallmark of cancer cells. Simultaneous inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis is critical to limit tumor aggressiveness and therapy resistance. Recent repositioning of FDA-approved antifungal azoles in oncology highlights their translational potential. However, the antitumor activity and mechanistic basis of butoconazole remain unexplored, and no clinical studies have yet examined butoconazole or related azoles in liver cancer. Here, by integrating transcriptomic, biochemical, and functional assays, we identify butoconazole as a dual disruptor of mitochondrial functionality -via inhibition of Complex II and V- and of glycolytic metabolism in liver cancer, ultimately collapsing cellular bioenergetics. This metabolic exhaustion was accompanied by (i) altered autophagic flux and (ii) a marked suppression of proliferation, clonogenicity, and migration across multiple hepatocellular carcinoma cell lines, ultimately limiting tumor growth in vivo without systemic toxicity at the tested dose. Mechanistically, BN induces inflammatory, oxidative stress, and ATF4-dependent pathways, while downregulating canonical survival signaling, and nucleoporin genes linked with poor prognosis. Collectively, these findings position butoconazole as an efficient candidate for drug repositioning in hepatocellular carcinoma by targeting tumor metabolic flexibility and energy homeostasis.

title: Exosome MS4A8 promotes bone metastasis in prostate cancer by activating NF-κB and AKT pathways through RANKL
abstract: Abstract Bone metastasis is the primary cause of death in patients with prostate cancer (PCa). In this study, we aimed to explore the mechanism by which MS4A8 mediates bone metastasis via exosomes. First, exosome proteome sequencing and detection of exosome MS4A8 expression revealed that MS4A8 was highly expressed in PCa exosomes and closely related to bone metastasis. Then, in vitro and in vivo experiments further showed that exosome MS4A8 could trigger osteolytic destruction in PCa bone metastases by enhancing the activity of osteoclasts. Furthermore, techniques such as ScRNA-seq, multicolour immunofluorescence, and co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) further revealed that exosome MS4A8 activates the nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT) pathways in osteoclasts of PCa bone metastases through receptor activator of nuclear factor-κB ligand (RANKL) and promoted osteoclast differentiation, resulting in a vicious cycle. Our study could provide a theoretical basis for clarifying the underlying mechanism of the occurrence and development of PCa bone metastasis and for future development of therapeutic strategies.

title: NF-κB–mediated chemoresistance emerges from distorted fallopian tube cell-state trajectory in ovarian cancer
abstract: Abstract Homeostatic gene expression programs persist through oncogenesis, creating new malignant states that adapt to therapies. To reveal how fallopian tube epithelia (FTE) cell states transform into intra-tumoral heterogeneity in ovarian high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC), we analysed treatment-naive tumors ( n = 50) and normal FTE ( n = 14) by single cell transcriptomics, identifying tissue-specific transcriptional modules gained, lost, or conserved through carcinogenesis. Of these, two conserved, opposing modules associated with survival and showed genetic biases, suggesting that oncogenic drivers employ existing epithelial programs. Challenging the cancer stem cell paradigm, a developmentally early oxidative-phosphorylation module was associated with improved survival, whereas the developmentally late MAPK/NF-κB module defined a stable, chemoresistant state that had lost the MHC II antigen presentation of the corresponding normal FTE state. Using these modules to predict perturbations capable of shifting cell-state dynamics, we demonstrate in patient-derived organoid models that restraining ER stress via SERCA2 activation drives a resistant, NF-κB–active phenotype, whereas inhibiting the DNA repair regulator CCDC6 promotes the opposite, platinum-sensitive state. Our study suggests that conserved tissue-of-origin states, rather than de novo cancer states, drive the key cell state dynamic and clinical response heterogeneity of HGSC and can be targeted in vitro to modulate platinum response.

title: DAPK1 orchestrates Lipin1-dependent fatty acid oxidation to enhance ferroptotic susceptibility in colorectal cancer
abstract: Abstract Metabolic reprogramming of lipid metabolism and redox homeostasis critically determines ferroptosis susceptibility in colorectal cancer (CRC), yet the upstream regulatory mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we identify death-associated protein kinase 1 (DAPK1) as a key regulator of Lipin1-dependent lipid metabolism and redox-controlled ferroptosis in CRC. Genetic and pharmacological analyses in CRC cells show that DAPK1 stabilizes Lipin1 and promotes its nuclear localization, thereby enhancing fatty acid oxidation (FAO). DAPK1-driven FAO activation increases lipid peroxidation, disrupts redox balance, and sensitizes CRC cells to ferroptosis, resulting in suppressed cell proliferation and migration. Consistently, DAPK1 overexpression restrains tumor growth in vivo, whereas DAPK1 deficiency accelerates tumor progression. Collectively, these findings reveal the DAPK1–Lipin1–FAO axis as a previously unrecognized metabolic redox vulnerability that can be exploited to induce ferroptosis in CRC.

title: A syngeneic mouse model of metastatic hormone-naive prostate cancer provides a platform for studying combination immunotherapy
abstract: Abstract Metastatic hormone-naive prostate cancer (mHNPC) refers to a small subset of diagnosed prostate tumors and presents very high mortality and poor response to available therapies. Despite its clinical relevance, we lack immunocompetent models that are both androgen-dependent and reliably metastatic, limiting the implementation of translational research strategies. Here we develop and characterize PL051, a syngeneic, bioluminescence tractable prostate carcinoma cell line derived from a Pten / Lkb1 double knockout genetic mouse model that reproducibly engrafts orthotopically in C57BL/6 mice, maintains androgen-receptor (AR) signaling, and consistently disseminates to soft tissues and bone. PL051 preserves Pten / Lkb1 loss and PI3K–AKT activation, shows intact AR responsiveness in vitro, and responds to AR-pathway intensification in vivo. We provide two complementary proof-of-concept evidence for the preclinical potential of this model. On one hand, we show the therapeutic benefit of combining androgen signaling inhibition and anti-PD1 treatment. On the other hand, we provide evidence showing that co-targeting myeloid cells with a CSF1R inhibitor further enhances therapeutic activity of checkpoint blockade by depleting suppressive macrophages and boosting T-cell recruitment. Together, this preclinical model fills a critical gap for studying mHNPC biology and provides a scalable, immune-competent model for testing rational combinatorial treatments.

title: Redox Orchestration of organ regeneration
abstract: Abstract The evolutionary transition from anaerobic to aerobic life imposed significant oxidative challenges, while also enabling the emergence of reactive oxygen species (ROS) as key regulators of cellular signaling.
