This review synthesizes current knowledge on how ROS, once considered merely toxic byproducts, have been co-opted as essential signaling molecules that orchestrate organ regeneration across phylogenetically diverse species. We highlight the biphasic nature of ROS—acting as promoters of regeneration at physiological levels but as inhibitors at pathological concentrations—and explore how this duality has been shaped by evolutionary pressures. Comparative analyses reveal that species with high regenerative capacity exhibit precise spatiotemporal control of ROS dynamics, often linked to flexible redox homeostasis and telomerase activity. In contrast, mammals exhibit stricter antioxidant regulation and telomerase restriction, which may underlie their limited regenerative potential and propensity for fibrotic repair. We further discuss the interplay between oxygen-sensing pathways, antioxidant systems, and ROS-mediated signaling networks in modulating regenerative outcomes. Understanding these evolutionary and mechanistic principles offers novel insights for developing redox-based therapeutic strategies to enhance tissue repair in humans.

title: PRMT6–SIRT5–HADHA signaling safeguards osteoblasts from R-loop-induced DNA damage during age-related osteoporosis
abstract: Abstract Age-related osteoporosis is characterized by impaired bone formation and progressive deterioration of trabecular microarchitecture. Declining osteoblast abundance and function, together with the accumulation of cellular senescence, are recognized as key contributors to skeletal aging. During aging, increased genomic instability and persistent DNA damage responses further impair osteogenic capacity. Aberrant accumulation of R-loops (RNA–DNA hybrids) can induce transcription–replication conflicts and DNA damage; however, the regulatory mechanisms maintaining R-loop homeostasis during osteoblast aging remain largely unknown. SIRT5, a key mitochondrial desuccinylase that regulates metabolic adaptation through protein lysine desuccinylation, has been implicated in cellular stress responses, but whether SIRT5 controls R-loop homeostasis and bone aging through succinylation remodeling remains unclear. Public mouse bone marrow single-cell RNA-seq datasets from GEO were integrated to delineate age-dependent changes in bone marrow cellular composition and the osteoblast lineage. Naturally aged mice as well as Sirt5 −/− and Prmt6 −/− models were analyzed, and skeletal phenotypes were assessed by micro-computed tomography and histological examination. In vitro, primary osteoblasts were subjected to replicative senescence and H₂O₂-induced oxidative stress. RNA-seq, lysine succinylation proteomics, S9.6-based R-loop CUT&Tag, Western blotting, and immunofluorescence were employed to characterize molecular alterations and phenotypic outcomes. Causality was further tested using AAV5-mediated Sirt5 overexpression in vivo and in vitro as rescue approaches. Single-cell analysis revealed a reduction in the proportion of osteoblasts during aging accompanied by decreased Sirt5 expression. Compared with wild-type controls, Sirt5 −/− mice exhibited more pronounced trabecular bone loss and impaired osteogenesis, with reduced Runx2, ALPL, and OCN and elevated p16/p21, decreased ALP activity, and increased SA-β-gal-positive cells. Transcriptomic profiling indicated activation of stress-related programs and suppression of osteogenic and metabolic pathways. Mechanistically, Sirt5 deficiency caused global succinylation accumulation and reshaped the succinylation landscape of metabolic proteins, leading to elevated multi-site succinylation of HADHA and reduced HADHA protein abundance. Concurrently, R-loops were broadly increased around transcription start site (TSS) regions, accompanied by elevated S9.6 and γH2AX signals and enhanced DNA damage accumulation. Prmt6 deficiency downregulated Sirt5 and phenocopied Sirt5 loss, including trabecular deterioration and increased R-loop signals. AAV5-mediated Sirt5 overexpression restored HADHA expression, attenuated R-loop accumulation and senescence phenotypes induced by oxidative stress or Prmt6 loss, and alleviated trabecular bone loss. Together, these findings identify the PRMT6–SIRT5 axis as a critical regulator of osteoblast aging. Disruption of this pathway promotes succinylation remodeling, compromises R-loop homeostasis, and enhances DNA damage accumulation, thereby accelerating osteoblast senescence and age-related bone loss. Targeting the PRMT6–SIRT5 signaling pathway may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for preventing osteoporosis associated with aging.

title: Pharmacologic CFTR potentiation attenuates alveolar epithelial senescence and experimental pulmonary fibrosis
abstract: Abstract Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a deadly lung disease that urgently requires effective treatments. A major factor driving IPF is the aging of alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells, which disrupts epithelial homeostasis and promotes fibrotic remodeling. Lungs from IPF patients exhibit reduced expression of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR), particularly in AT2 cells, which typically have high CFTR levels. It remains unclear whether acquired CFTR dysfunction contributes to the development of IPF. This study examines whether the CFTR potentiator VX-770 (ivacaftor) can reduce experimental pulmonary fibrosis by targeting AT2 cell senescence. In a bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis mouse model, VX-770 treatment reduced pulmonary fibrosis by limiting collagen deposition and restoring normal lung structure and function. The treatment reestablished epithelial homeostasis, decreasing aberrant KRT8 + transitional cells and preventing the loss of alveolar type 1 cells. Notably, VX-770 diminished cellular senescence both in vivo and in AT2 cell organoid cultures by decreasing the expression of senescence markers and the pro-fibrotic senescence-associated secretory phenotype. Notably, deleting CFTR specifically in AT2 cells lessened the therapeutic effect of VX-770, confirming its target-specific action. Mechanistically, VX-770 stabilized the CFTR-PTEN protein complex, elevating PTEN levels and thereby inhibiting the profibrotic PI3K/AKT signaling pathway. Overall, these findings identify acquired CFTR dysfunction as a key druggable driver of pulmonary fibrosis, providing preclinical evidence supporting the repurposing of VX-770 as a novel senescence-targeting therapy for IPF.

title: miRNA cargo from pleural mesothelioma-derived extracellular vesicles reprograms fibroblasts toward an inflammatory CAF-like phenotype
abstract: Abstract Pleural mesothelioma (PM) is an aggressive cancer with a low survival rate. A better understanding of disease pathogenesis can aid the development of therapies. This study profiles the miRNA cargo of PM-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) and examines their effects on fibroblasts, the predominant cell type in the PM tumour microenvironment (TME). High-throughput profiling revealed that EVs from epithelioid and non-epithelioid PM have distinct miRNA cargoes differing from each other and from non-malignant controls. Our data suggest that oncogenic miRNAs were upregulated and tumour-suppressive miRNAs were downregulated in PM-derived EVs. Further, we identified miRs that are exclusively present in either epithelioid or non-epithelioid PM subtypes. These miRs could serve as biomarkers to distinguish PM subtypes and aid in treatment decisions. To analyse the EV-mediated fibroblast response, fibroblasts were treated with isolated EVs, followed by RNA-seq and molecular analyses. Our miRNA–mRNA integrative analysis predicts that differential miRNA cargo from PM-derived EVs modulates multiple pathways in treated fibroblasts. GSEA analysis on KEGG_2021_Human and oncogenic signatures predicts upregulation of pathways including Cell Cycle, Neutrophils and Extracellular Trap Formation, and EZH2-Regulated pathways in treated fibroblasts. Through molecular analysis, we report that a predominant inflammatory CAF-like phenotype was observed post-EV treatment, as reflected by increased levels of markers like IL-6/8, MMP-1/3, ICAM1, ENG, and RRAGD. This was also accompanied by enhanced oncogenic signalling reflected by elevated Osteopontin, thrombospondin, Cystatin C, autotaxin, AXL, and ERBB2 levels. Additionally, our data show that PM-EVs modulate epigenetic regulation by altering EZH2 phosphorylation at Thr345: epithelioid EVs increased p-EZH2 levels, and non-epithelioid EVs decreased p-EZH2 levels. Further, our data show that PM-EV-mediated fibroblast reprogramming can increase PM cell migration and proliferation, thus promoting a tumour-supportive microenvironment. Collectively, this study highlights the regulatory roles of PM-EVs. The predicted EV-driven signalling pathways in PM-TME may represent potential therapeutic avenues for future therapeutic research.

title: STF-62247 induces a non-canonical, caspase-independent cell death in ccRCC associated with autophagic and lysosomal dysfunction
abstract: Abstract Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), the most prevalent form of kidney cancer, is driven by early chromosome 3p loss and VHL inactivation, frequently followed by secondary mutations in other 3p genes, such as SETD2, PBRM1, and BAP1 . The small molecule STF-62247 was found to target VHL -deficient ccRCC through autophagy-dependent cell death. We recently demonstrated that SETD2 inactivation in VHL -reconstituted ccRCC cells also confers vulnerability to STF-62247, accompanied by caspase-3 and gasdermin E (GSDME) cleavage. Here, we investigated the underlying cell death mechanisms that drive STF-62247 cytotoxicity across different ccRCC genetic profiles. Our results ruled out necroptosis, ferroptosis, and GSDMD-mediated pyroptosis. In VHL -deficient cells, signature markers of classical intrinsic apoptosis, including cytochrome c release, PARP, and caspase-3 cleavage, as well as the extrinsic apoptosis marker, caspase-8 cleavage, were induced with STF-62247. Conversely, SETD2 -inactivated cells did not display cytochrome c release or caspase-8 activation. CRISPR knockout of CASP3 or GSDME , or pharmacological inhibition of caspases, failed to rescue cell death, proving these pathways are secondary. Mechanistically, immunofluorescence for LAMP1, cathepsin L (CTSL), and Galectin-3 indicated the absence of lysosomal membrane permeabilization. Instead, STF-62247-mediated PIKfyve inhibition caused endolysosomal enlargement, trapping immature pro-CTSL within non-functional compartments. We hypothesize that cells may alter their autophagic machinery to cope with this degradative arrest, potentially leading to an atypical secretory autophagy-like response; this could account for the observed LAMP1 plasma membrane translocation in VHL-deficient cells and dysfunctional vacuolar accumulation in SETD2-deficient models. Genetic ablation of ATG5 or BECN1 or pharmacological inhibition of autophagy with SAR405 partially rescued viability in SETD2 -inactivated cells, confirming that this autophagy-linked pathway actively contributes to cell death. Collectively, we found that STF-62247 triggers a multifaceted cell death program associated with autophagic machinery deregulation. While GSDME cleavage does not dictate survival, its pro-inflammatory potential remains an intriguing perspective to be explored for potentially optimizing immunotherapy strategies in ccRCC.

title: DYRK1A coordinates tumor–stroma secretory programs that promote an immunosuppressive microenvironment in pancreatic cancer
abstract: Abstract Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by a desmoplastic, immunosuppressive stroma dominated by cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs). Paracrine signals from cancer cells and CAFs shape the tumor microenvironment (TME), facilitating interactions that drive tumor growth and immune evasion, yet the molecular regulators of this crosstalk remain incompletely understood. Here, we show that Dual-specificity Tyrosine-Regulated Kinase 1 A (DYRK1A), previously shown to promote PDAC growth by stabilizing c-MET in cancer cells, is also expressed in CAFs at levels comparable to those in cancer cells. Secretome profiling of DYRK1A-depleted cancer cells and CAFs by quantitative mass spectrometry revealed DYRK1A-dependent factors in each cell type associated with terms related to cell migration, while combining the DYRK1A-regulated proteins from both compartments highlighted additional categories associated with immune infiltration and cell-cell interactions in the TME. Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of DYRK1A reduced CCL2, CCL5, and CSF-1 secretion in cancer cells, and CXCL12 in CAFs, linking DYRK1A activity to immunosuppressive paracrine signaling. Conditioned media from DYRK1A-depleted cancer cells or CAFs impaired the migration of monocytes and myeloid-derived suppressor cells, indicating that DYRK1A remodels the PDAC secretome to recruit immunosuppressive myeloid populations. These findings extend the established role of DYRK1A beyond cancer cell-intrinsic signaling, highlighting its role as a regulator of secreted factors that shape the PDAC TME, and position this kinase as a potential target to reduce immunosuppressive signaling.

title: JNK-mediated RAD18 phosphorylation promotes colorectal cancer progression through K48-linked ubiquitination and degradation of SFN
abstract: Abstract Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality, highlighting the need to further elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying its progression. RAD18, an E3 ubiquitin ligase with established roles in DNA damage tolerance and tumor progression, is aberrantly expressed in multiple malignancies; however, the substrate-specific mechanisms underlying its tumor-promoting function in CRC remain incompletely understood. In this study, we investigated the functional and molecular roles of RAD18 in CRC using public datasets, clinical specimens, CRC cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and xenograft models. Protein interactions and ubiquitination were examined using co-immunoprecipitation, mass spectrometry, cycloheximide-chase, and ubiquitination assays, together with mutant constructs and functional rescue experiments. RAD18 was significantly upregulated in CRC and was associated with poor prognosis. RAD18 promoted CRC cell proliferation and cell-cycle progression, whereas its depletion induced G2/M arrest. Mechanistically, RAD18 interacted with SFN through its RING domain and catalyzed K48-linked ubiquitination of SFN at lysine 122 (K122), leading to its proteasomal degradation. JNK-mediated phosphorylation of RAD18 at serine 409 (S409) enhanced the RAD18–SFN interaction and subsequent SFN ubiquitination. Functional analyses using the phosphorylation-deficient RAD18-S409A mutant and the ubiquitination-resistant SFN-K122R mutant further supported a critical role for phosphorylation-regulated SFN degradation in the proliferative and cell-cycle effects of RAD18. Collectively, these findings identify a JNK–RAD18–SFN regulatory axis in which RAD18-mediated SFN degradation attenuates SFN-dependent G2/M checkpoint control, facilitates G2/M progression, and promotes CRC growth.

title: MCP-1 licenses mesenchymal stem cells for T-cell-supportive function
abstract: Abstract Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) exhibit dynamic immunomodulatory capacity, transitioning between immunosuppressive and immunosupportive states in response to microenvironmental cues. However, the molecular signals that regulate this functional plasticity across diverse MSC populations remain poorly defined. Here, we report that monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) promotes a T-cell-supportive phenotype in selected MSC populations (such as MSCs from bone marrow, adipose tissue, pancreas, and gingiva). In CTX-induced immunosuppressed mice, MCP-1-pretreated selected MSCs protected T cells from apoptosis and partially restored lymphoid organ atrophy. In vitro, MCP-1 inhibited IFN-γ binding to TLR2 and promoted CXCL10 expression in LNMSCs, supporting T-cell survival and proliferation. SPR confirmed dose-dependent MCP-1–TLR2 binding, and molecular dynamics simulations provide a computational structural rationale for this interference. These findings identify MCP-1 as a promoter of T-cell-supportive function in selected MSC populations, with responses dependent on tissue source and cellular context.

title: Excess bile acid impairs oocyte maturation through H1.2-mediated chromatin and epigenetic remodeling
abstract: Abstract Oocyte development requires precise coordination between metabolic and epigenetic programs, yet how metabolic disturbances affect chromatin regulation remains unclear. Here, we identify a mechanistic link between bile acid metabolism and oocyte maturation. Excess cholic acid (CA) impairs meiotic progression and spindle assembly, accompanied by a marked depletion of linker histone H1.2. Quantitative proteomics and functional assays reveal that H1.2 insufficiency drives chromatin decompaction and loss of H3K27me3, leading to defective meiotic apparatus assembly and increased aneuploidy. CUT&Tag profiling further identifies genome-wide redistribution of H3K27me3 at promoters of WNT signaling and kinase-regulatory genes. Restoring H1.2 expression reinstates both chromatin organization and meiotic fidelity in CA-treated oocytes. These findings suggest that H1.2 is a chromatin-associated factor associated with oocyte quality and that excess cholic acid compromises oocyte competence, at least in part, through H1.2-mediated epigenetic remodeling. This metabolic-epigenetic coupling provides mechanistic insight into infertility associated with cholestasis, polycystic ovary syndrome, and other metabolic disorders.

title: PHF2-mediated hydroxylation destabilizes NFATc1 to restrain osteoclastogenesis
abstract: Abstract Osteoclast differentiation requires not only the induction of osteoclastogenic gene expression but also the removal of inhibitory regulators that limit lineage progression. Although transcriptional brakes on osteoclastogenesis have been described, whether post-translational brakes similarly limit NFATc1 accumulation remains unclear. Here, we identify plant homeodomain finger protein 2 (PHF2), a Jumonji C (JmjC) domain-containing lysine demethylase, as a post-translational brake on osteoclast differentiation and osteoclast-driven bone loss. PHF2 expression progressively declined during RANKL-induced osteoclastogenesis, whereas myeloid-specific Phf2 deletion enhanced osteoclast formation and trabecular bone loss. Conversely, PHF2 gain-of-function suppressed osteoclast differentiation. PHF2 directly associated with NFATc1 and catalyzed K612 hydroxylation in vitro, facilitating HUWE1-dependent ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of NFATc1. Consistent with this mechanism, the K612A substitution stabilized NFATc1 and enhanced osteoclastogenesis. In an ovariectomy model of postmenopausal osteoporosis, myeloid Phf2 deficiency further aggravated trabecular bone deterioration and osteoclast activity in vivo. Collectively, these findings identify the PHF2–NFATc1–HUWE1 axis as a previously unrecognized post-translational brake on osteoclast differentiation, with mechanistic implications for osteoclast-driven bone loss.

title: Mechanical stress promotes osteoarthritis progression by increasing miR-145a-5p secretion through Piezo1
abstract: Abstract Exosomal microRNAs (miRNAs) are key mediators of intercellular communication and contribute to disease progression, while exosome generation and release can be regulated by mechanical stimuli. Piezo1 is a pivotal mechanosensitive ion channel involved in mechanotransduction; however, how mechanical forces influence exosome-associated signaling and osteoarthritis (OA) progression through Piezo1 remains unclear. In this study, tensile stress was applied to chondrocytes to investigate Piezo1 activation and its downstream effects. Mechanical loading activated Piezo1 and increased intracellular calcium signaling, accompanied by enhanced activation of the transcription factor NFATc1 and increased miR-145a-5p expression. Functional and mechanistic analyses demonstrated that miR-145a-5p directly targeted and suppressed Forkhead box protein O1 (FoxO1), thereby promoting chondrocyte degeneration. Chondrocyte-specific conditional deletion of Piezo1 in Piezo1 flox/flox ; Col2a1 CreERT mice reduced miR-145a-5p expression and attenuated cartilage degeneration in an OA model. Conversely, intra-articular overexpression of miR-145a-5p aggravated cartilage degeneration, whereas inhibition of miR-145a-5p markedly alleviated chondrocyte degeneration and delayed OA progression. Analyses of human osteoarthritic cartilage and longitudinal plasma miRNA data further supported the clinical relevance of miR-145-5p in OA-associated pathological changes. Collectively, these findings identify a mechanotransduction pathway in which mechanical overload activates Piezo1-mediated calcium signaling and NFATc1, leading to increased miR-145a-5p expression and subsequent suppression of FoxO1. Targeting the Piezo1–NFATc1–miR-145a-5p–FoxO1 axis may therefore provide a potential therapeutic strategy for mechanically driven OA.

title: DDX49 drives colorectal cancer progression by remodeling mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation via PGC-1α binding
abstract: Abstract Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a highly prevalent and aggressive malignancy worldwide. Dysregulation of mitochondrial metabolic homeostasis critically contributes to CRC progression, yet the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain incompletely characterized. Using multi-omics analyses, we demonstrate that enhanced mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) is a prominent metabolic feature of CRC, and identify the DEAD-box helicase DDX49 as a novel regulator of mitochondrial metabolism. DDX49 is aberrantly upregulated in CRC tissues, and its high expression correlates with advanced clinicopathological stages and adverse patient prognosis. In vitro and in vivo assays showed that DDX49 promotes CRC cell proliferation, clonogenicity, tumor growth and suppresses cellular apoptosis. Mechanistically, nuclear DDX49 directly binds to and stabilizes peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ coactivator 1-α (PGC-1α), which in turn upregulates TFAM and OXPHOS complex subunits, thereby enhancing mitochondrial respiratory function. Rescue assays further confirm that PGC-1α serves as an essential downstream mediator of DDX49. Collectively, our study reveals that DDX49 drives CRC progression via the DDX49–PGC-1α–OXPHOS regulatory axis, and highlights DDX49 as a promising prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target for CRC.

title: Dhx36 modulates the G-quadruplex within the Alpl promoter to promote osteogenesis and ameliorate osteoporosis
abstract: Abstract G-quadruplexes (G4s) are non-canonical nucleic acid structures that play important roles in diverse biological processes and represent promising therapeutic targets. However, their role in osteogenic differentiation remains largely unexplored. Here, we show that G4 abundance decreases during osteogenic differentiation and that pharmacological stabilization of G4 structures impairs osteogenesis in both cellular and animal models. We further identify a G4 structure within the promoter of the key osteogenic gene alkaline phosphatase (Alpl) as a critical cis-regulatory element governing osteogenic differentiation. Mechanistically, the topology of the Alpl G4 is dynamically modulated by the G4-binding proteins Nucleolin and Dhx36. Nucleolin stabilizes the Alpl G4, thereby suppressing Alpl promoter activity, whereas Dhx36 modulates the Alpl G4, resulting in the activation of Alpl transcription. Moreover, adeno-associated virus-mediated Dhx36 gene therapy effectively restored bone mass in ovariectomy-induced osteoporotic mice. Collectively, these findings establish G4 structures as key regulators of osteogenic differentiation and highlight modulation of G4 dynamics through Dhx36 as a promising therapeutic strategy for osteoporosis.
